displayQuote: Writers Are Just Schmucks with Underwoods

meta.title: Who really said "Writers Are Just Schmucks with Underwoods"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Not Samuel Goldwyn. The earliest evidence, from 1961, points to Jack L. Warner — and it says "typewriters", not "Underwoods".
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'Writers Are Just Schmucks with Underwoods'?
meta.ogDescription: Quote Investigator dates the first evidence to 1961 and Jack Warner. The Goldwyn credit turns up in 1986, and QI calls it inadequately supported.

answer.label: Not Samuel Goldwyn — the thin evidence points to Jack L. Warner
answer.authorDates: 1892–1978 · Canadian-born American studio chief, president of Warner Bros.
answer.sourceLine: Quote Investigator ↗ finds the earliest evidence in 1961, in the journalist Bill Davidson’s Hollywood memoir The Real and the Unreal: “one of the Warner brothers” called all his writers, William Faulkner included, “schmucks with typewriters.” Faulkner worked for Jack Warner, so that is who Davidson meant. Two things keep it from being firm. Davidson published a second version months later saying “schleps”, which QI says “reduces the credibility of the ascription”; and the brand-name form on this page — “Underwoods” — does not appear in print until 1976. The Goldwyn credit is later still, and QI calls it inadequately supported.

source.heading: Where the line actually comes from

docMeta.dd: Bill Davidson, The Real and the Unreal (Harper & Brothers, 1961), p. 242
Robert Kirsch, Los Angeles Times, 25 July 1976, p. B1
Bernard McTigue, American Book Collector 7, no. 4 (April 1986), p. 55

source.excerpt: One of the Warner brothers, for example, used to call all writers—even William Faulkner, who was once under his command—“schmucks with typewriters” (schmuck is a derisive Yiddish expression for a bumpkin, an idiot). He used to make all his writers punch a time clock as they entered and left the studio…
trail: 1961 — the first evidence, in Bill Davidson’s The Real and the Unreal ↗, chapter 14, p. 242. The remark is “schmucks with typewriters” and the speaker is “one of the Warner brothers”, identifiable as Jack L. Warner ↗ because Faulkner was under contract to him. Quote Investigator ↗ treats this as the strongest link.

1961, again — Davidson repeats the anecdote in Show: The Magazine of the Arts that October with “schleps with typewriters”. QI ↗: “It is unclear why Bill Davidson presented two different quotations, and the inconsistency reduces the credibility of the ascription.”

25 July 1976 — the Underwood ↗ brand enters the saying. Robert Kirsch, reviewing a book in the Los Angeles Times, writes that “Jack Warner was reputed to have snarled that writers were just ‘schmucks with Underwoods’”. It is repeated as Warner’s in his Washington Post obituary in 1978 and by Michiko Kakutani in the New York Times in 1982, all per QI ↗.

1986 onward — the credit starts drifting to other moguls. American Book Collector gives it to Sam Goldwyn in April 1986; The Partisan Review gives it to “Lewis B. Mayer” in 1987; Ben Stein gives it to Harry Cohn in 2011. QI’s verdict ↗ on all three: “inadequately supported.”
source.cutTag: Bill Davidson, The Real and the Unreal, 1961, p. 242
source.excerptNote: That is the whole of the earliest evidence, and it names nobody directly. In October of the same year Davidson reworked the passage for Show magazine and printed the same anecdote with “schleps with typewriters” instead. QI ↗ notes the inconsistency and suggests the taboo weight of the Yiddish word may explain the swap — but either way one journalist giving two wordings is not a firm ascription. The passage is quoted from QI’s transcription; the 1961 book is lending-restricted on the Internet Archive and we could not read it ourselves.

source.rightsNote: We assert no rights status. This is a reported insult, not a passage from an authored work, and the wording on this page cannot be tied to a specific publication before 1931. The earliest printings we can name — a 1961 book and a 1976 newspaper column — are both after the United States public-domain threshold and are themselves in copyright as texts. Quote it as reportage.

author.name: Jack L. Warner
author.heading: The mogul the trail actually leads to
author.metaLine: 1892–1978 · Canadian-born American studio chief, president of Warner Bros.
author.bio: Jack Leonard Warner, born Jacob Warner in London, Ontario, ran Warner Bros. in Burbank for a career spanning more than fifty-five years — longer than any of the other founding Hollywood moguls. He is the brother in the phrase “one of the Warner brothers”, and the one William Faulkner was under contract to during his screenwriting years, which is what makes him the identifiable subject of the 1961 anecdote. He was known for blunt and off-colour remarks; his 1978 Washington Post obituary printed this one as though it were settled fact. It is not quite that, but it is the only version of the story with a contemporary source behind it.

Both cited in “Quote Origin: Writers Are Just Schmucks with Underwoods,” Quote Investigator, 2 April 2014.

misattribution.heading: Four moguls have been credited with this
misattribution.intro: It is a line about contempt for writers, so it has been attached in turn to almost every mogul famous for showing it. Only one of the four has a contemporary source behind him, and even that source contradicts itself.

items.why: First credited to Goldwyn in Bernard McTigue’s “Cat Chat” column in American Book Collector, April 1986 — twenty-five years after the earliest evidence, and with nothing behind it. QI ↗: the later attributions to Goldwyn, Mayer and Cohn “were inadequately supported.”

Bill Davidson’s The Real and the Unreal ↗ puts “schmucks with typewriters” in the mouth of “one of the Warner brothers” who employed Faulkner. That is Jack Warner ↗. It is indirect, it does not name him, and it does not say “Underwoods” — but it is the only strand with a source.
The Partisan Review gave it in 1987 to “Lewis B. Mayer”, almost certainly a garbling of Louis B. Mayer. QI ↗ finds no support for it.
Ben Stein attributed it to the Columbia Pictures chief in 2011. QI ↗ finds no support for that either.

The brand name is not in the 1961 evidence. It first appears in the Los Angeles Times of 25 July 1976 ↗, fifteen years later, in a sentence that already treats the remark as legend (“was reputed to have snarled”).

misattribution.truthLine: If you must attach a name to it, attach Jack L. Warner’s ↗ — and say “reportedly”. Quote Investigator’s chronology ↗ shows the Goldwyn credit arriving in 1986, twenty-five years after the first evidence and with nothing new behind it.

context.heading: Why the studios needed a phrase for this
lead: The insult exists because the arrangement it describes was real. Studios hired the best writers in America, paid them extraordinarily well, and then treated them as interchangeable staff — Davidson’s 1961 passage goes straight from the epithet to the detail that mattered: “He used to make all his writers punch a time clock as they entered and left the studio.” Faulkner punched that clock. So, at various points, did Dorothy Parker, George S. Kaufman and Raymond Chandler.

The brand name is what made the phrase travel. Underwood ↗ built the first widely successful modern typewriter and had made five million machines by 1939; naming it turned a generic sneer into a picture of a room. That is probably also why the wording drifted toward it — and why the version with the brand in it, which nobody has ever tied to a named speaker at the time, is the one everybody now quotes.
context.detailsSummary: The riposte, and where the line went next
detailsBody: Writers took the phrase over almost immediately. Page Stegner used it on himself in The Atlantic Monthly in 1977 (“I’m going back to being a schmuck with an Underwood”); William Goldman used it in the 1998 edition of The Princess Bride; Larry Gelbart answered it in the New York Times in 1997 with “You remember Shakespeare. He was that schmuck with a quill.” A 2007 letter to Time closed the circle: “It might also be fair to say that Mr. Warner was just a schmuck with a Rolodex.” All of these are documented in QI’s chronology ↗.

The Yiddish word itself moved around. Davidson printed “schmucks” in his book and “schleps” in his magazine article the same year; and the 1992 book Fatal Subtraction reports the news anchor Peter Jennings saying “schnooks” on air, congratulating Art Buchwald after his win over Paramount — QI gives no date for that broadcast. QI ↗ notes that “schmuck” is the form that recurs, and records a reader’s observation that its vulgar etymology may be why a magazine of the early 1960s would have softened it.
context.pull: The earliest evidence says “typewriters”. The famous version says “Underwoods”, and arrives fifteen years later.

schema.verdictNote: Commonly credited to Samuel Goldwyn, which Quote Investigator calls inadequately supported. The earliest evidence, from 1961, points to Jack L. Warner, but it is indirect, it does not name him, and it gives the wording as “schmucks with typewriters” rather than “Underwoods”. Treat the attribution to Warner as the best available, not as established.

sourcesVerified.claim: Quote Investigator's earliest evidence is Bill Davidson, The Real and the Unreal (Harper & Brothers, 1961), chapter 14, p. 242: 'One of the Warner brothers, for example, used to call all writers—even William Faulkner, who was once under his command—"schmucks with typewriters"... He used to make all his writers punch a time clock'. Davidson printed 'schleps with typewriters' in Show magazine, October 1961, and QI states 'the inconsistency reduces the credibility of the ascription'. The 'Underwoods' wording first appears in Robert Kirsch, Los Angeles Times, 25 July 1976, p. B1; the Goldwyn credit in Bernard McTigue, American Book Collector 7:4 (April 1986), p. 55; 'Lewis B. Mayer' in The Partisan Review (1987); Harry Cohn in Ben Stein (2011). QI concludes: 'the evidence in 1961 indicated that Jack Warner could be credited with calling writers "schmucks with typewriters"... Later attributions to Samuel Goldwyn, Louis B. Mayer, and Harry Cohn were inadequately supported.'

Wikipedia states Jack Leonard Warner (born Jacob Warner; August 2, 1892 – September 9, 1978) was a Canadian-born American film executive who was president and driving force behind Warner Bros. Studios in Burbank, with a career spanning over 55 years, surpassing any other of the pioneering Hollywood studio moguls.

Wikipedia's Samuel Goldwyn article states that 'Goldwynisms were the inventions of humorists and newspaper editors' and that 'Many famous "Goldwynisms" predate Goldwyn's career as circulated witticism'.

Wikiquote's Samuel Goldwyn page has a Misattributed section listing nine fake Goldwynisms (verbal contract, comedies not to be laughed at, im-possible, include me out, Indians from the reservoir, next time I send a damn fool, read part of it, psychiatrist, Western Union) and does NOT list 'schmucks with Underwoods' among them or anywhere else on the page.

Wikipedia states the Underwood Typewriter Company was an American manufacturer headquartered in New York City with manufacturing in Hartford, Connecticut, that produced what is considered the first widely successful modern typewriter, and that by 1939 Underwood had produced five million machines.

Internet Archive holds a catalogue record for Bill Davidson, The Real and the Unreal (1961), the book carrying the earliest evidence. The item is marked access-restricted and the full text was not read here; the transcription above is Quote Investigator’s.
